channel.description: Recent content in Design Patterns on wid's blog

item.title: Microservices Architecture
item.description: MSA is a decision about which criterion to use to decompose the system. Domain boundary, data ownership, scale pattern, failure isolation — the chosen criterion creates the service boundaries, and those boundaries decide communication and data in turn.

item.title: Event Sourcing and CQRS
item.description: ES and CQRS are decisions about the form of the source of truth and the separation of its views. Changing the form of truth shifts the entire system design, so adoption must explicitly account for the cost.

item.title: Circuit Breaker
item.description: A Circuit Breaker’s trip trigger and recovery strategy must be designed together. Trip without recovery cuts the dependency permanently; recovery without a trip basis becomes meaningless cycling.

item.title: Rate Limiting
item.description: Before choosing a rate limit algorithm, the protection layer decides which algorithms are even available. This post lays out how L4/L7/Application layers and Token/Leaky/Sliding/Fixed algorithms intersect.

item.title: Builder
item.description: Builder is the answer when three limits of constructors meet at once — many parameters, some optional, and step-wise validation. With fewer than all three, simpler tools suffice. When the language provides rich named/default parameters, the need for Builder shrinks as well.

item.title: Factory
item.description: Factory’s shared intent is separating creation from use. The three variants — Factory Method, Abstract Factory, and Static Factory Method — split creation differently and suit different conditions. Static Factory Method is the variant most often encountered in practice, and DI containers absorb part of Factory’s explicit role.

item.title: Singleton
item.description: Singleton is one of the simplest patterns but the canonical anti-pattern debate. The decision to bundle single-instance guarantee with global access into one pattern causes tight coupling and test difficulty. DI is the general alternative that separates the two intents.

item.title: Dependency Injection — The Hierarchy of DIP, IoC, and DI
item.description: DIP (principle), IoC (pattern), and DI (technique) sit at different levels of abstraction. The hierarchy must be clear before framework features and design principles can be told apart.
